objectives: Derive SIR + SEIR dynamics from first principles + interpret R₀ + Re.
Compute herd-immunity thresholds + reason about variants + waning.
Compare contact tracing, NPIs, + lockdown evidence across 1918, HIV, Ebola, COVID-19.

slides.title: SIR + SEIR: the equations of an epidemic
slides.body:
**Kermack + McKendrick (1927)** — 'A Contribution to the Mathematical Theory of Epidemics' (Proc Roy Soc A). Three compartments + two transition rates produced an epidemic curve that fit historical plague + cholera outbreaks. Almost a century later, the same equations underlie every modern outbreak forecast.

**SIR model** (well-mixed population, frequency-dependent transmission):

  dS/dt = -β · S · I / N
  dI/dt = β · S · I / N - γ · I
  dR/dt = γ · I

- **S** = susceptible; **I** = infectious; **R** = recovered (or removed); N = S+I+R.
- **β** = effective contact rate × per-contact transmission probability (units: per time).
- **γ** = 1/D, where D = infectious duration (units: per time).
- **R₀ = β/γ** = basic reproduction number = mean secondary cases generated by one infected person in a fully susceptible population (Anderson + May 'Infectious Diseases of Humans' 1991 — the canonical textbook).

**Threshold behavior**: epidemic spreads if dI/dt > 0 initially, i.e., β·S/N > γ, i.e., R_eff = R₀·S/N > 1. As S falls, R_eff falls → epidemic peaks when R_eff = 1, i.e., S/N = 1/R₀.

**Effective reproduction number** R_e (or R_t) = R₀ · S/N · (interventions). Time-varying; estimable from case data with delays + reporting noise via EpiEstim (Cori 2013) or Wallinga-Teunis.

**SEIR model** adds an **Exposed** (E) compartment for the latent period before becoming infectious:

  dS/dt = -β · S · I / N
  dE/dt = β · S · I / N - σ · E
  dI/dt = σ · E - γ · I
  dR/dt = γ · I

σ = 1/L, where L = mean latent period. For COVID-19: L ≈ 3-5 days (latent) + D ≈ 5-7 days (infectious). For measles: L ≈ 8 days + D ≈ 5 days.

**Generation interval (G)** = time between infection events in transmission pairs. R₀ ≈ exp(r·G) for small growth rate r (van Kerkhove + Wallinga). Used to translate doubling time → R₀.

**Extensions used in modern outbreak modeling**:
- **Age-structured** (heterogeneous mixing matrices; POLYMOD contact surveys; Mossong 2008).
- **Stochastic + branching processes**: matter at small population numbers + onset of outbreaks (super-spreading; Lloyd-Smith 2005).
- **Spatial / metapopulation**: GLEAM (Vespignani), MOBS Lab models.
- **Waning immunity + reinfection** (SEIRS): COVID-19 with variant escape.
- **Vaccination compartment** (V): SEIRV.
- **Hospitalization + ICU compartments**: needed for capacity planning.

slides.title: Herd immunity + R₀ + variants
slides.body:
**Herd immunity threshold (HIT)** = critical fraction immune to drive R_e < 1 in a fully mixed population:

  HIT = 1 - 1/R₀

- **Measles** (R₀ ≈ 12-18): HIT ≈ 92-95%. Why measles requires >95% MMR coverage.
- **Mumps** (R₀ ≈ 5): HIT ≈ 80%.
- **Pertussis** (R₀ ≈ 5-7, with waning immunity): HIT ≈ 80-85%.
- **Smallpox** (R₀ ≈ 3.5-6): HIT ≈ 70-85% — why eradication was achievable.
- **Polio** (R₀ ≈ 5-7): HIT ≈ 80-86%.
- **Seasonal flu** (R₀ ≈ 1.3): HIT ≈ 23% — but waning + variant drift prevent stable HI.
- **COVID-19 ancestral** (R₀ ≈ 2-3): HIT ≈ 50-66%; **Alpha** (R₀ ≈ 4-5): HIT ≈ 75-80%; **Delta** (R₀ ≈ 5-7): HIT ≈ 80-86%; **Omicron BA.1+** (R₀ ≈ 8-12): HIT ≈ 88-92% with full sterilizing immunity — never achievable with non-sterilizing vaccines + immune escape.

**Why herd immunity is more subtle in practice**:
- **Heterogeneity** in contact rates → herd-immunity threshold lower than (1 - 1/R₀) when high-contact individuals are infected first. Britton + Trapman (2020) Science: heterogeneity in COVID-19 may have lowered effective HIT to ~40-50% during ancestral wave.
- **Spatial + demographic clustering** → local outbreaks despite high overall immunity (Brooklyn measles 2019, Samoa measles 2019).
- **Waning immunity** (pertussis aP; flu; SARS-CoV-2) → HI is transient.
- **Variant escape** (Omicron) raises effective R₀ + reduces vaccine effectiveness against infection.
- **Vaccines reduce severity even when they don't prevent infection** → policy goal shifts from elimination → suppression + protection of severe disease.

**Anderson + May (1991) 'Infectious Diseases of Humans'**: the canonical textbook of mathematical epidemiology. Roy Anderson + Robert May (later Lord May, ecologist + UK Chief Scientific Advisor) brought ecological + mathematical rigor to infectious disease modeling, including HIV, BSE, foot-and-mouth disease.

**Estimating R₀ from data**:
- **Final size relation**: R₀ = -ln(S_∞/S_0) / (1 - S_∞/S_0) — invert from final attack rate.
- **Initial growth**: r = (R₀ - 1)/D → R₀ = 1 + r·D.
- **Real-time methods**: Wallinga-Teunis 2004; EpiEstim Cori 2013; renewal equation framework.
- **Cautions**: super-spreading events + heterogeneity inflate variance; reporting delays + ascertainment bias distort estimates.

slides.title: Contact tracing + NPIs + the historical record
slides.body:
**Test-Trace-Isolate (TTI)** — when R₀ is moderate (~2-4) + a substantial fraction of transmission is symptomatic, contact tracing can suppress an outbreak. Effective if (a) high test sensitivity + rapid turnaround; (b) ~50%+ contact-tracing coverage within 2-3 days; (c) effective quarantine of contacts. Hellewell + Funk (CMMID 2020) modeled COVID-19 TTI viability — concluded high tracing coverage + rapid action could control R_t < 1 for ancestral strain but became infeasible at high incidence + with substantial pre-symptomatic transmission.

**Non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs)** during epidemics:
- **Personal**: masks, hand hygiene, respiratory etiquette, isolation of cases.
- **Community**: closing schools, restricting gatherings, work-from-home.
- **Travel restrictions** (debated; modest effect on incubation-period-length disease).
- **Lockdowns**: stay-at-home orders + business closures.

**Ferguson + Imperial Report 9** (Mar 16 2020) — modelled COVID-19 in UK + US assuming R₀ ~2.4; predicted ~510k UK + 2.2M US deaths absent intervention; ~1.1M US + 250k UK with mitigation; near-elimination with strict suppression. Drove UK lockdown + US emergency response. **Flaxman + Bhatt + Imperial team (2020 Nature)** — Bayesian hierarchical model of European lockdowns; estimated ~3.1M deaths averted by NPIs in 11 European countries through May 2020; lockdowns the dominant single intervention.

**1918 H1N1 influenza pandemic** — 'Spanish flu'; ~50M deaths worldwide, ~675k US deaths. Hatchett + Mecher + Lipsitch (PNAS 2007) — historical NPI comparison: cities with earlier + more sustained social distancing (St Louis vs Philadelphia) had lower peak mortality + similar cumulative mortality. Foundational evidence base for NPI planning.

**HIV/AIDS** — pandemic emerged ~1980; transformed from death sentence to chronic disease 1996+ with HAART. Key insights:
- **Combination therapy** — single agents → resistance; 3+ drug regimens (Ho + Markowitz 1995-96).
- **U=U (Undetectable = Untransmittable)** — viral suppression to <200 copies/mL eliminates sexual transmission (Cohen HPTN 052 2011; PARTNER 2016; PARTNER2 2019). Treatment as prevention.
- **PrEP** (TDF/FTC Truvada, oral 2012; long-acting cabotegravir 2021 Delany-Moretlwe HPTN 084).
- **Voluntary medical male circumcision** (Auvert 2005; Bailey 2007; Gray 2007) — 50-60% reduction in male HIV acquisition; programmatic scale-up in eastern + southern Africa.
- **PEPFAR + Global Fund** financing the scale-up.
- **PMTCT** — vertical-transmission reduction from ~30% to <2% with ART + delivery interventions.

**Ebola West Africa 2014-2016** — Guinea + Liberia + Sierra Leone; ~28k cases + ~11k deaths. R₀ ≈ 1.5-2 in early phase. Lessons: weak health-system surveillance + delayed WHO declaration; community engagement + safe-burial practices critical; rVSV-ZEBOV vaccine (ring vaccination trial Henao-Restrepo 2015) developed under emergency. Set up the **Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI 2017)**.

**MERS-CoV 2012+** — Saudi Arabia camel reservoir; ~2500 cases + 866 deaths; CFR ~35%. Notable for hospital-amplified transmission + South Korea 2015 outbreak (186 cases).

**SARS 2002-2003** — ~8000 cases + 774 deaths; CFR ~10%; contained within 6 months via classical TTI + case isolation (no community transmission once recognized). Demonstrated that aggressive case-based control could end a respiratory outbreak with R₀ ~2-3.

**Zika 2015-2016** — congenital Zika syndrome (microcephaly); Brazil outbreak; vector-control + travel advisories. Reaffirmed link between arboviruses + neurological development.

**COVID-19 (2019-)** — emerged Wuhan late 2019; declared PHEIC Jan 30 2020 + pandemic Mar 11 2020. >7M reported deaths; estimated excess mortality 14-20M (WHO; The Economist). Variants of concern: Alpha (UK 2020-Q4), Delta (India 2021), Omicron (South Africa 2021-Q4). Defining features: pre-symptomatic transmission, super-spreading, mRNA + viral-vector vaccines deployed within 1 year (Operation Warp Speed; Pfizer-BioNTech BNT162b2; Moderna mRNA-1273; Oxford-AZ ChAdOx1), Long COVID syndromes.

slides.title: Interactive: explore the SIR epidemic curve
slides.body:
Use the interactive epidemic-curve visualization to develop intuition about how R₀, initial conditions, + intervention timing change the trajectory of an outbreak.

**What to try**:
- Set R₀ = 1.0 → flat / fizzle (R_e ≤ 1).
- Set R₀ = 1.5 → slow exponential (early HIV-like growth rate).
- Set R₀ = 2.5 → COVID-19 ancestral; ~50-60% attack rate without intervention.
- Set R₀ = 12 → measles; >95% attack rate; only suppressed by very high immunity.
- Toggle SIR vs SEIR to see the role of latency.

**Key observations**:
- Peak prevalence + total attack rate are both increasing functions of R₀.
- Final attack rate satisfies the implicit equation 1 - S_∞/S_0 = 1 - exp(-R₀ · (1 - S_∞/S_0)) — the **final-size relation**.
- Even R₀ = 1.5 yields ~58% attack rate eventually without intervention — small R₀ does not mean small outbreak.
- Adding latency (SEIR) delays the peak but doesn't change final size (in the closed-population, no-intervention case).
- Reducing transmissibility late in the wave has small effect on final size; early intervention is dramatic.

Use the visualization to test counterfactuals: would moving the intervention 2 weeks earlier have averted what fraction of cases? This kind of reasoning is at the heart of real-world outbreak response.

question.question: From SIR equations to herd-immunity threshold
question.goal: Derive the herd-immunity threshold for measles + COVID-19 ancestral + Omicron from R₀ + interpret why measles requires >95% MMR.

steps.prompt: Write the condition for an epidemic to grow (dI/dt > 0) at the start.
steps.reveal: dI/dt = β·S·I/N - γ·I > 0 ⟺ β·S/N > γ. At S ≈ N (start of epidemic), this becomes β > γ, i.e., R₀ = β/γ > 1.

steps.prompt: When does the epidemic cease to grow (dI/dt = 0)?
steps.reveal: dI/dt = 0 when β·S/N = γ ⟺ S/N = γ/β = 1/R₀. At that moment, R_e = R₀ · S/N = 1. The fraction immune is 1 - S/N = 1 - 1/R₀ = HIT (herd immunity threshold).

steps.prompt: Compute HIT for measles (R₀ ≈ 15), ancestral COVID-19 (R₀ ≈ 2.5), Omicron (R₀ ≈ 10).
steps.reveal: Measles HIT = 1 - 1/15 ≈ 93.3% → why MMR coverage must be >95% (with vaccine effectiveness ~97%, that gives ~92% immune ≈ HIT). Ancestral COVID-19 HIT = 1 - 1/2.5 = 60%. Omicron HIT = 1 - 1/10 = 90%. Real-world COVID-19 herd immunity unattainable with non-sterilizing vaccines + variant escape + waning — but high coverage still cuts hospitalizations + deaths.

steps.prompt: Why does the simple HIT formula overestimate the threshold in practice?
steps.reveal: When contact rates are heterogeneous, highly-connected individuals get infected first; the remaining susceptibles have lower mean contacts → effective R_e drops faster than the naive formula predicts. Britton + Trapman (Science 2020) estimated this could lower COVID-19 HIT to ~40-50% during ancestral wave. Conversely, vaccination targeted at high-contact groups boosts herd protection more than uniform vaccination.

steps.prompt: Why does the formula underestimate the threshold for COVID-19 vaccination programs?

acceptedAnswers: waning immunity + variant escape + vaccine not sterilizing

hints: What if vaccine doesn't fully prevent infection?
steps.reveal: If vaccine effectiveness against infection is V_e (e.g., 50% for Omicron post-3 months), the immune-equivalent coverage is V_e × C. Even at 100% coverage, V_e = 50% gives 50% effective immunity — insufficient. Plus, waning + variant escape erode immunity over months. So pure 'herd immunity' via vaccination became infeasible for COVID-19; policy goal shifted to preventing severe disease (which vaccines do well, ~90% effectiveness against severe disease).

question.question: An outbreak shows a 3-day doubling time during exponential growth. Mean generation interval is ~5 days. What's the approximate R₀?
options: R₀ cannot be estimated from doubling time.
question.explanation:
Growth rate r = ln(2)/T_d = 0.693/3 ≈ 0.231/day. With generation interval G ≈ 5 d + assuming roughly exponentially-distributed infectious period, R₀ ≈ 1 + r·G ≈ 1 + 0.231·5 ≈ 2.15.

A more accurate formula using the **Lotka-Euler equation** for a gamma-distributed G: R₀ = exp(r·G) ≈ exp(1.16) ≈ 3.2. The 'true' answer depends on the assumed distribution of the generation interval; values between 2 + 3 are reasonable. This is the doubling-time → R₀ conversion used widely during COVID-19; the Wallinga-Lipsitch (2007) paper formalized it. Caution: doubling time depends on testing capacity ramps + reporting delays — real-time R_e estimates from EpiEstim (Cori 2013) are usually more reliable.

slides.workedSolution: r = ln(2)/3 = 0.231/d. R₀ ≈ 1 + r·G = 1 + 0.231·5 ≈ 2.2 (linear approx) or exp(r·G) ≈ 3.2 (exponential approx). Order-of-magnitude R₀ ≈ 2-3.

question.question: Outbreak response: novel respiratory pathogen with R₀ ≈ 2.5 + 30% pre-symptomatic transmission
question.prompt: A novel respiratory pathogen with R₀ ≈ 2.5, mean generation interval ~5 d, 30% pre-symptomatic transmission, CFR ~1% (age-skewed), no vaccine yet. You are the national PH lead. Discuss: (a) the role + limits of test-trace-isolate given pre-symptomatic transmission (Hellewell + Funk modeling); (b) timing + intensity of NPIs (school closures, masks, gathering limits, mobility restrictions) using Imperial Ferguson + Flaxman-Bhatt evidence; (c) how SEIR modeling would inform peak ICU + deaths under different intervention scenarios; (d) cross-border + travel policy; (e) parallel vaccine + therapeutics R&D; (f) communication + counter-misinformation strategy; (g) equity considerations — who bears NPI burden (essential workers, low-income, schoolchildren); (h) exit strategy + how vaccination scale-up shifts the policy from suppression to mitigation.

question.question: Measles R₀ ≈ 16 in a fully susceptible population. What's the herd-immunity threshold (fraction of the population that must be immune)? Express as a percentage.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain why R₀ alone is insufficient to predict an outbreak's trajectory + which additional quantities (generation interval, dispersion k, heterogeneity, immunity structure) matter — using COVID-19 + measles as contrasting examples.
question.rubric: Mentions: R₀ gives mean secondary infections in fully susceptible population; but generation interval (G) determines speed (doubling time); dispersion parameter k captures super-spreading (Lloyd-Smith 2005) — low k (e.g., COVID-19 k ≈ 0.1-0.5) means most transmission from few super-spreaders + chains often die out stochastically (matters for control); heterogeneity in contact + susceptibility lowers effective HIT below 1 - 1/R₀ (Britton + Trapman); immunity structure (waning, variant escape, age + risk distribution) determines whether HIT is achievable. Contrast: measles R₀ ≈ 16, low dispersion (more homogeneous transmission), long-lasting immunity → HIT achievable + maintainable via MMR. COVID-19 R₀ ≈ 2-10 by variant, high dispersion, waning + variant escape → HIT not stable; policy aim shifted to severe-disease prevention. Conclude: R₀ is one parameter among many; modeling needs the full quartet.
